source_title: Predictably Irrational: The Hidden Forces That Shape Our Decisions (Revised and Expanded Edition)
author: Dan Ariely
concept: Relativity: we judge value by comparison, not in absolute terms
summary: Ariely opens with the finding that humans rarely judge things on absolute worth; we evaluate options relative to whatever is next to them. The cheap-pen versus expensive-suit example shows we will drive across town to save $7 on a $15 pen but not on a $1,000 suit, even though the saved dollars are identical.
usable_principle: Because buyers judge relatively, the comparison set you place an option in controls how its value is perceived. Frame the alternatives deliberately rather than presenting a price in isolation.
sniped_relevance: When BJ prices or presents any offer, the surrounding comparison set shapes perceived value as much as the number itself; set the frame on purpose. author: Dan Ariely
concept: The decoy effect: an asymmetrically dominated option steers the choice
summary: The Economist subscription study: adding a clearly inferior third option (a print-only price equal to the print+web price) made most people pick the more expensive bundle. A decoy nobody chooses still reshapes which real option looks best by giving the buyer an easy relative comparison.
usable_principle: A well-placed decoy (an option that is strictly worse than the target) raises the chosen value without changing the target's price. Design the option menu, not just the prices.

source_title: Predictably Irrational: The Hidden Forces That Shape Our Decisions (Revised and Expanded Edition)
author: Dan Ariely
concept: Arbitrary coherence: the first price anchors all later willingness to pay
summary: The social-security-number auction showed bids tracked the (random) last two digits of participants' SSNs: high-digit groups bid 216 to 346 percent more for the same goods. Initial prices are arbitrary, but once lodged they make all later prices cohere around the anchor (the Tom Sawyer / Assael pearls insight).
usable_principle: The first number a buyer sees becomes the reference point for everything after. Set the initial anchor consciously, because it has a long, self-reinforcing tail.
sniped_relevance: BJ's first published price or rate for any service quietly anchors what clients expect to pay later; the opening number is a long-term decision, not a throwaway. source_title: Predictably Irrational: The Hidden Forces That Shape Our Decisions (Revised and Expanded Edition)
author: Dan Ariely
concept: The high cost of zero cost: FREE is an emotional trigger, not a price point
summary: Ariely's Hershey's-Kiss / Snickers and Amazon free-shipping experiments show that dropping a price to zero causes a disproportionate, irrational surge in demand. People over-choose the free item even when a small-cost alternative is objectively better value; zero removes the felt downside of loss.
usable_principle: FREE is the most powerful lever in an offer because it eliminates perceived risk, but it distorts behavior; deploy it where it genuinely serves the buyer, not to bait a worse choice.
sniped_relevance: A free lead magnet, sample shoot, or trial can pull disproportionate response for whatever BJ builds; the lever is real and should be used honestly, not to trap. source_title: Predictably Irrational: The Hidden Forces That Shape Our Decisions (Revised and Expanded Edition)
author: Dan Ariely
concept: Social norms versus market norms: introducing money rewrites the relationship
summary: Ariely shows we operate in two worlds: social exchange (favors, goodwill, no ledger) and market exchange (priced, calculated). Mixing them backfires: offering to pay your mother-in-law for Thanksgiving dinner, or naming a price in a courtship, damages the relationship and cannot easily be undone.
usable_principle: Once a transaction is framed in market norms, social goodwill evaporates and is hard to recover. Decide deliberately which norm a given interaction runs on.

concept: Run customer relationships on social norms where it fits, not pure market norms
summary: The flip side of the social/market-norm finding: companies that treat customers with social-norm generosity (genuine goodwill, going beyond the contract) earn loyalty that priced, purely transactional relationships never buy, but the moment they break trust by reverting to hard market norms (fees, penalties), the social bond collapses.
usable_principle: Build the customer relationship on social norms when you want loyalty, but honor them consistently; a single market-norm betrayal (a surprise fee) resets the whole relationship to transactional.

author: Dan Ariely
concept: The hot-cold empathy gap: we underpredict how emotion hijacks our decisions
summary: Ariely's arousal study found people in a calm state badly underestimate how differently they will decide when aroused or emotional, by margins of 70 to 136 percent. Every participant, however rational, became 'divorced from the person he thought he was' under the influence of passion.
usable_principle: Decisions made in a cold state do not survive a hot state; the reliable defense is to commit to rules in advance rather than trusting in-the-moment judgment.
sniped_relevance: BJ should make consequential choices (pricing floors, scope limits, what to say yes to) as cold-state rules, because the heat of a sales conversation or a tense moment predictably distorts judgment. concept: Procrastination and self-control: external commitment beats willpower
summary: Ariely's deadline experiments showed students who were given (or imposed on themselves) firm, spaced deadlines performed far better than those left to self-regulate. We systematically sacrifice long-term goals to immediate impulses; pre-committed structure, not resolve, is what closes the gap.
usable_principle: Do not rely on willpower for recurring goals; build external commitment devices (deadlines, structures, defaults) that make the desired behavior the path of least resistance.

source_title: Predictably Irrational: The Hidden Forces That Shape Our Decisions (Revised and Expanded Edition)
author: Dan Ariely
concept: The endowment effect: we overvalue what we already own
summary: The Duke basketball-ticket study: students who won tickets in a lottery valued them roughly 14x higher than students who lost (about $2,400 to sell versus $175 to buy), though both groups had camped equally. Ownership, plus loss aversion and the focus on what we would give up, inflates perceived value.
usable_principle: People price their own things far above what others will pay; expect this gap in any negotiation, trade-in, or 'try it free then keep it' flow, and account for the owner's loss aversion.
sniped_relevance: When BJ values his own work, time, or assets, the endowment effect can inflate the internal number; pricing to the market means consciously correcting for owner bias. concept: Keeping doors open: we irrationally pay to preserve options, and closing them focuses
summary: Ariely contrasts the Chinese commander Xiang Yu (who burned his ships and crushed the cooking pots to force victory) with normal behavior: in the door-clicking experiment people spent real resources to keep dying options alive rather than commit to the best one. We hate foreclosing alternatives even when keeping them open costs more than they are worth.
usable_principle: Optionality has a hidden running cost; deliberately closing weak doors concentrates resources and attention on the option that actually pays. Commit rather than hedge by default.

concept: The placebo of price: a higher price can raise the real perceived effect
summary: The Veladone (vitamin C sold as a painkiller) and SoBe (full-price versus discounted energy drink) experiments: the higher-priced version produced measurably stronger effects, less pain, better puzzle performance, because price itself signals quality and triggers a real placebo response. Discounting can unconsciously lower the experienced value.

source_title: Predictably Irrational: The Hidden Forces That Shape Our Decisions (Revised and Expanded Edition)
author: Dan Ariely
concept: The context of our character: honest people cheat a little, and moral reminders stop it
summary: Ariely's matrix and token experiments (the 'fudge factor') found most people cheat by a small amount when they can rationalize it, and that cost-benefit or odds-of-getting-caught barely move the needle. What sharply reduces cheating is a moral reminder (recalling the Ten Commandments, signing an honor code) right before the temptation.
usable_principle: Dishonesty is mostly small-scale self-deception, not calculated risk; the lever that protects integrity is a salient reminder of values at the moment of temptation, not heavier penalties.
sniped_relevance: BJ can design systems (his own and clients') that keep behavior honest by surfacing values and clear standards at decision points, rather than relying on surveillance or penalties; this is the honest use of the finding.
